newsitem.title: USA: Balanced zinc concs market in near term -Brook Hunt.
newsitem.headline: Balanced zinc concs market in near term -Brook Hunt.

text.p: The zinc concentrate market is set to remain largely balanced over the next three years despite a sharp increase in mined output coming on stream, analyst Huw Roberts of Brook Hunt said.
"Our near term outlook assumes a relatively balanced market with no extreme movements in concentrate stocks," Roberts said.

Following a modest deficit in 1996, small surpluses of less than 100,000 tonnes were expected in 1998 and 1999, Roberts told the American Zinc Association conference which met in Arizona earlier this week.

Western World concentrate production is expected to rise significantly between 1996 and 1999, lifting total output to nearly 6.3 million tonnes of contained zinc, almost 800,000 tonnes, or 14 percent, more than last year.
"There are more than adequate mineable reserves to meet any conceivable increase in demand for the forseeable future," Roberts said.

But unless zinc's fortunes improve significantly over the next two to three years to spur new mine projects, there may well be shortages of concentrates from the start of the next decade when a large number of mines are due to close, Roberts added.
In the West the demand for concentrates will rise by 700,000 tonnes of contained zinc by 1999 from last year, but this depends on a string of announced smelter expansion projects coming on stream.
But Brook Hunt still believed that the demand for concentrates in the West will not be able to consume all the extra mined output coming on stream.
However, any concentrate surplus will be limited by rising exports from the West to the Eastern Bloc countries, especially China.
"We expect exports to China to rise further over the next few years to reach perhaps 180,000 tonnes of zinc content in 1999," Roberts said.

China's ability to mine more concentrates itself will remain limited in the near term. Concentrates exports to nations formerly part of the Soviet Union will continue to decline to just under 40,000 tonnes by 1999.
